title: More Time in Light Could Reduce Dementia Risk
paragraphs: Dementia is becoming a serious global health challenge. In 2020, there were at least 55 million people around the world living with it.

But dementia mainly affects older people. And as improvements in other areas of health lead to longer lifespans, the number of people with dementia is expected to rise to 78 million by 2030, and 139 million by 2050.

Dementia isn't one single disease either. It can be caused by many different conditions — such as Alzheimer's disease — that are linked with an accumulation of waste proteins in the brain and a decline in cognitive function.

While there is no cure, research points to lifestyle interventions as having protective effects. And one study has found that just spending time in the sun may support brain health and reduce the risk of developing dementia.

The study, published in General Psychiatry, included almost 88,000 participants with an average age of 62, and who were all dementia-free at the outset of the research. They each wore a wrist device for seven days that measured their exposure to light during both the day and night.

After an average follow-up period of eight years, 741 participants had developed dementia. And the researchers found that being exposed to an average daytime light level above 1,000 lux was linked with a 16% lower risk of dementia.

A lux is a standard unit to measure light, and is based on how much light falls on a surface. One lux is about the same as how much a regular candle lights up one square meter around it — and 1,000 lux is the equivalent of light from the sun on a very overcast day.
Full sunlight can measure 100,000 lux or more.

And the study found that spending an average of at least 42 minutes in moderate daytime light of at least 5,000 lux was linked to a 17% reduced risk of dementia. Meanwhile, spending less than 42 minutes in 5,000 lux light was a greater predictor of dementia than alcohol consumption, which is a well-established risk factor.
